script.opening: (Mother, shaken.) "Doctor, this morning Musa just went stiff and started jerking and his eyes rolled back and I genuinely thought he was dying in my arms. It was the most terrifying thing of my life. He’s okay now, back to normal, but I’m petrified it’ll happen again, and — does this mean he’s got epilepsy? Has it damaged his brain? I can’t stop shaking. I don’t want to ever leave him alone again."

facts.text: If clarified: brief (~2 min), generalised, self-terminating convulsion during a fever, in a child aged 6 months–6 years, with full recovery — a classic SIMPLE febrile convulsion (generalised, brief, not repeated in the same illness, full recovery). He has a clear infective source (otitis media) and is now well, alert, feeding, neurologically normal.

Simple febrile convulsions are common, benign, do NOT cause brain damage, do NOT mean epilepsy (NICE NG217: febrile seizures tend not to predispose to later afebrile seizures; the large majority never develop epilepsy), and most children grow out of them by school age. Recurrence with later fevers is possible but does not change the benign outlook.

HIDDEN AGENDA — beneath the epilepsy/brain-damage questions is acute trauma and a specific terror: the mother witnessed something she thought was death, feels she "failed to protect him", and is developing hypervigilance (won’t leave him, won’t sleep). There may also be guilt that she "didn’t bring the fever down fast enough" — a misconception that antipyretics prevent febrile convulsions (they do not: NICE NG143). These need addressing or she’ll be paralysed by fear.
She doesn’t know what to DO if it happens again — the not-knowing fuels the terror. Concrete first-aid (recovery position, time it, when to call 999) restores some control.

Officially: to know if it’s epilepsy/brain damage and how to stop it recurring. What is needed: clear, warm reassurance about the benign nature, correction of the antipyretic/guilt misconception, concrete what-to-do-next-time first aid and safety-netting, and acknowledgement of the trauma.

ice.ideas: The convulsion may mean epilepsy or brain damage, and she should have brought the fever down faster to prevent it.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — trauma from witnessing what looked like her child dying, guilt at "failing to protect him", and developing hypervigilance/insomnia; terror of recurrence and of not knowing what to do.
ice.expectations: To be told whether it’s epilepsy/brain damage. What is actually needed: warm reassurance about the benign nature, correction of the guilt/antipyretic myth, concrete first-aid for any recurrence, and acknowledgement of the trauma.

cues: "I thought he was dying in my arms" — acute trauma; respond to the distress before the facts.
"Does it mean epilepsy / brain damage?" — the specific fears to address directly with clear reassurance.
"I should have brought his fever down faster" — the guilt and the antipyretic misconception to correct gently.

checkpoints.text: Identifies this as a SIMPLE febrile convulsion (brief, generalised, not repeated in the same illness, full recovery, young child with fever and an identified source; NICE NG217 notes that febrile seizures lasting longer than 10 minutes or with focal features may carry a higher risk of later epilepsy) and conveys that it is benign and common

Reassures accurately on the specific fears: simple febrile convulsions do NOT cause brain damage and do NOT equate to epilepsy (NICE NG217: febrile seizures tend not to predispose to later afebrile seizures; the large majority never develop epilepsy); most children outgrow them by school age

Corrects the antipyretic/guilt misconception: antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen) treat discomfort but do NOT prevent febrile convulsions and should not be used for that purpose (NICE NG143), and nothing she did or didn’t do caused it — directly lifting the self-blame

Gives concrete FIRST AID for any recurrence: protect from injury, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, place in the recovery position when jerking stops, TIME the seizure, and call 999 if it lasts 5 minutes or more (NICE NG217 defines convulsive status epilepticus as a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more), is the second in the same illness or within 24h, focal, or there are concerning features (breathing difficulty, not recovering)

Knows what would make it COMPLEX/atypical and warrant different management/referral: prolonged (more than 10 minutes — NICE NG217), focal, recurrent within 24h or the same illness, incomplete recovery, age outside 6mo–6y, or diagnostic uncertainty/meningitis features — and that the underlying fever source still needs appropriate treatment, with the NICE NG143 traffic-light approach and sepsis considered (NICE NG254)
Responds to the TRAUMA first — acknowledges how terrifying it was, validates the "I thought he was dying" experience — before delivering reassurance; paces the consultation to her distress
Addresses the hypervigilance and guilt with compassion, normalising her reaction and gently heading off paralysing over-protection, offering support if the trauma persists

Safety-nets and supports: written information on febrile convulsions and first aid (NICE NG217: information on the risk of further seizures, how to get help, and safety advice), explicit 999 criteria, advice on the current infection, who to contact with worries, and follow-up — leaving her informed, equipped and calmer rather than terrified

worked.txt: "Before any medical explanation — what you went through this morning sounds genuinely terrifying. Watching your baby go stiff and jerk and thinking he was dying is one of the most frightening things a parent can experience, and it’s completely understandable that you’re still shaking. You did not do anything wrong. Let’s take this gently."

"Here’s what happened, and it’s genuinely reassuring: Musa had what we call a febrile convulsion — a seizure triggered by a fever in a young child. They look horrifying, but they are common — lots of young children have one — and the important part: they do NOT cause brain damage, and they are NOT epilepsy. He is not brain-damaged and he almost certainly does not have epilepsy."

"And this matters — you said you should have brought his fever down faster. Please hear me: nothing you did or didn’t do caused this. Calpol and ibuprofen help a child feel more comfortable, but they do NOT prevent these convulsions — that’s a really common belief and it’s simply not true. You did not fail to protect him. This was not your fault."

"Most children grow out of these by the time they’re at school. It can happen again with another fever — some children do have another — but that doesn’t change the good news: still benign, still not epilepsy, still no harm to him. Knowing it might recur isn’t meant to frighten you; it’s so you’re prepared rather than blindsided."

"So here’s exactly what to do if it ever happens again, because not knowing is half the terror: keep him safe from knocking into anything, don’t hold him down and don’t put anything in his mouth, and when the jerking stops, roll him onto his side. Look at a clock and time it. Call 999 if it has lasted five minutes, happens twice in the same illness, or he doesn’t come round properly. Most stop on their own within a couple of minutes, like this one did."

"I’ll send you written information so you’re not relying on memory. Keep treating his ear infection as we discussed. And it’s okay if you don’t sleep well for a few nights — that’s the shock. But you don’t need to watch him every second; he’s well now and back to himself. If the fear is still gripping you in a week or two, come back and we’ll help with that too. You handled something terrifying and your boy is absolutely fine."

f.learning: A brief, generalised, self-terminating convulsion during a fever in a child aged 6 months–6 years with full recovery and an identified source is a SIMPLE febrile convulsion — benign, common, NOT brain damage, and NOT epilepsy (NICE NG217: febrile seizures tend not to predispose to later afebrile seizures; most never develop epilepsy), with most children outgrowing them by school age. The clinical tasks are to confirm the simple pattern, know what makes it complex/atypical (prolonged — more than 10 minutes per NICE NG217 — focal, recurrent in 24h or the same illness, incomplete recovery) and warrant referral, and treat the underlying infection. But this is overwhelmingly a COMMUNICATION case: respond to the parent’s trauma first ("I thought he was dying"), correct the pervasive guilt-laden misconception that antipyretics prevent febrile convulsions (they do not — NICE NG143; nothing she did caused it), and give concrete recurrence first aid (protect, don’t restrain, recovery position, time it, 999 at 5 minutes — NICE NG217 — or a second seizure in the same illness or incomplete recovery) so the not-knowing terror is replaced by control. Acknowledge the hypervigilance, offer follow-up, and provide written information.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG143 (fever in under 5s) · NICE NG217 (epilepsies, 2022, updated January 2025) · NICE NG254 (sepsis, under 16s)
knowledge.summary: A brief, generalised, self-limiting seizure during a fever in a young child who recovers fully is a simple febrile seizure. It is frightening to watch but benign. The consultation is mostly about the parent’s shock, guilt and what to do next time.

points.t: Simple: generalised, brief, not repeated in the same illness, with full recovery. Complex features: focal, lasting longer than 15 minutes, repeated within the same illness or incomplete recovery. Complex febrile seizures carry a somewhat higher risk of later epilepsy and need paediatric assessment.

NICE NG217: febrile seizures tend not to predispose to later afebrile seizures, unlike a first afebrile seizure. A single simple febrile seizure does not mean epilepsy and does not harm the brain. Recurrence with later fevers is possible, and most children grow out of them.

NICE NG143: antipyretic agents do not prevent febrile convulsions and should not be used specifically for this purpose. Use them only for a distressed child. This directly answers the parent’s guilt that she “should have got the fever down faster”.

points.h: Look for the cause of the fever
points.t: Confirm the source (here, otitis media) and exclude serious infection. Features such as a non-blanching rash, neck stiffness, a bulging fontanelle, persistent drowsiness or incomplete recovery need urgent assessment. Use the NICE NG143 traffic-light approach and consider sepsis (NICE NG254).

Protect from injury, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, note the time, and place in the recovery position once the jerking stops. NICE NG217 defines convulsive status epilepticus as a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more: call 999 at 5 minutes, or for a second seizure in the same illness, breathing difficulty or failure to recover.

NICE NG217: give parents information about the risk of further seizures, how to seek help if one happens, and safety advice to reduce the risk of injury. Written information is essential after such a frightening event.

First child, shock, sleeplessness, fear of leaving him, who is at home to support her.
Observed on video that he is alert and playing; checked the earlier assessment; no investigations needed for a simple febrile seizure with a clear source.
Simple vs complex febrile seizure; considered meningitis, sepsis and non-febrile causes.
Asked about rash, neck stiffness, drowsiness, vomiting and further seizures; confirmed generalised, brief, full recovery.
Simple febrile convulsion with otitis media, explained in plain words as benign and not epilepsy.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Corrected the antipyretic myth (NICE NG143), gave recurrence first aid with 999 at 5 minutes (NICE NG217), continued ear treatment.
Addressed parental trauma and hypervigilance; offered follow-up for her own wellbeing.
Written information, named urgent features (non-blanching rash, drowsiness, stiff neck, breathing), return if trauma persists.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Lee. I’ve read the notes from this morning. Before anything else — how are you doing? It sounds like it was a frightening morning.
model.why: Opens with the parent’s experience rather than the medical facts

model.text: He went stiff and started jerking and his eyes rolled back, and I honestly thought he was dying in my arms. He’s fine now, but I can’t stop shaking. Is it epilepsy? Has it damaged his brain?

That sounds terrifying, and it makes complete sense that you’re still shaking. I’m going to answer both of those questions clearly. Can I first check how he is now, and hear a bit more about what happened? Then we’ll talk about what it means and what to do.
model.why: Validates the fear, promises answers and sets a clear agenda

model.text: Okay. Yes.
Is Musa with you? Can you turn the camera to him? How has he been since the doctor saw him this morning — eating, drinking, playing, responding to you as normal?
model.why: Confirms full recovery using video observation

model.text: He’s right here, playing. He’s eating and drinking. He’s back to himself — it’s me that isn’t.
He looks bright and busy, which is exactly what I want to see. During the fit, did both arms and legs jerk the same, or was it one side? And roughly how long did it last?
model.why: Establishes generalised vs focal and duration

model.text: All of him. About two minutes I think, though it felt like forever. Then he was really sleepy.
And since then: any rash, any stiff neck or dislike of light, vomiting, or has he been unusually sleepy or hard to wake? Any more fits?
model.why: Screens for meningitis, sepsis and recurrence

model.text: No, nothing like that. Just the ear. He’s on the treatment from yesterday.
You said it’s you that isn’t back to yourself. What’s been going through your mind since this morning?
model.why: Follows the cue to her own distress

model.text: That it’s my fault. I should have got his temperature down faster. And I don’t want to leave him alone again, not even to sleep. What if it happens and I don’t know what to do?
Thank you for telling me. That’s such a normal reaction after a shock like this. Let me take those one at a time — the guilt, what it means for him, and exactly what to do if it happens again.
model.why: Normalises the reaction and structures the concerns

model.text: Please.

What Musa had is called a febrile convulsion — a fit triggered by a rising temperature in a young child. It was short, it involved his whole body, it stopped by itself and he’s recovered completely. Those are the signs of the common, simple type.
model.why: Names the diagnosis and the features that make it simple

model.text: Your two big questions. It has not damaged his brain. And this is not epilepsy — a fit with a fever is a different thing from epilepsy, and the great majority of children who have one like this never develop epilepsy. Most children grow out of these as they get older.
model.why: Answers the specific fears directly and accurately

model.text: Not epilepsy. Okay. (Breathes out.) But the temperature…
This is important. Calpol and ibuprofen make a child more comfortable, but they don’t prevent these fits. Nothing you did or didn’t do caused it. You didn’t fail him — you held him through it.
model.why: Corrects the antipyretic myth and lifts the guilt (NICE NG143)

model.text: I really thought I’d let it happen.

It can happen again with another fever, so let me give you a plan. If he fits: put him somewhere he can’t hurt himself, don’t hold him down and don’t put anything in his mouth. Look at the time. When the jerking stops, roll him onto his side. Call 999 if it lasts five minutes, if he has another one in the same illness, or if he doesn’t come round properly.
model.why: Concrete first aid with explicit 999 criteria (NICE NG217)

model.text: Five minutes. Time it. On his side.

Exactly. Carry on with his ear treatment. Give Calpol or ibuprofen only if he seems uncomfortable. He doesn’t need watching every second — he can sleep in his own cot tonight. Checking on him as you normally would is enough.
model.why: Tailored plan that gently heads off hypervigilance

model.text: I don’t know if I’ll sleep, though.

A few bad nights after a shock like this is normal. If in a week or two you’re still getting flashbacks, can’t sleep or can’t leave him, please come back — that’s common after seeing something so frightening, and we can help with it.

I’ll send you written information on febrile convulsions and first aid, so you don’t have to remember it all. Please get help urgently if he becomes floppy or very drowsy, has a rash that doesn’t fade under a glass, a stiff neck, or is struggling to breathe.
model.why: Written information plus named urgent features

model.text: When you tell his dad tonight, what will you say happened and what you’d do next time?
That it was a fever fit, it’s not epilepsy, it didn’t hurt his brain, and it wasn’t my fault. If it happens: keep him safe, time it, on his side, 999 at five minutes.
That’s it exactly. You did everything right today.
model.why: Closes with reassurance that restores confidence

social.t: Witnessing a seizure is often experienced as watching a child die. Sleeplessness, hypervigilance and intrusive memories are common in the days after and deserve acknowledgement.
Ask who is at home tonight. Sharing the first-aid plan with the other parent and any regular carers (nursery, grandparents) spreads the load and the knowledge.

legal.t: No legal restriction follows a single febrile seizure. Parents may wish to share the first-aid plan with nursery staff; this is their choice and needs their consent.

professional.t: Reassurance must be accurate: say clearly it is not epilepsy and has not harmed him, while being honest that it can recur (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: give information patients can understand).
A video follow-up is appropriate after an in-person assessment, but any new drowsiness, rash or further seizure needs face-to-face or emergency care. Document the advice given.

community.t: Written febrile convulsion and first-aid information; health visitor support for a first-time parent; paediatric first-aid courses (for example British Red Cross or St John Ambulance).

redFlags: Focal or prolonged seizure, a second seizure in the same illness, or incomplete recovery — complex features needing urgent assessment
Non-blanching rash, neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle, persistent drowsiness — meningitis or sepsis (NICE NG143, NICE NG254)
Seizure lasting 5 minutes or more — 999 (NICE NG217)
psychosocial: First child; parent in shock and not sleeping
Fear of leaving him alone, even to sleep
Who is at home tonight to support her
ice: Idea: “Is it epilepsy? Has it damaged his brain? I should have got the fever down.”
Concern: it will happen again and she won’t know what to do
Expectation: a clear answer about epilepsy and brain damage

playbook.diagnosis: Simple febrile convulsion in an 18-month-old with acute otitis media: brief, generalised, self-terminating, single, with full recovery. No features of complex seizure or meningitis.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Musa had a fever fit — some young children’s brains react to a quickly rising temperature by having a short fit. It looks awful, but it doesn’t damage the brain, it isn’t epilepsy, and most children grow out of them.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been blaming yourself for not bringing his temperature down. Please hear this: medicines for fever don’t stop these fits. Nothing you did caused it.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the trauma, normalise a few bad nights, discourage constant watching, and offer a review for her if flashbacks or sleeplessness persist.
sharedPlan: Continue treatment for otitis media; antipyretics only for comfort (NICE NG143), doses per BNFC
First aid for recurrence: protect, don’t restrain, time it, recovery position, 999 at 5 minutes (NICE NG217)
Written information on febrile convulsions and first aid
safetyNet: 999 for a seizure lasting 5 minutes, a second seizure, not recovering, or breathing difficulty
Urgent help for non-blanching rash, stiff neck, floppiness or drowsiness; return if her distress persists

pitfalls.intro: The clinical content here is simple. The station is failed on sequence and tone: facts delivered to a parent still in shock, hedged answers to her two big questions, and a guilt that nobody lifts.

items.fail: Opening with “febrile convulsions are common and benign” before acknowledging what she saw.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” She cannot hear reassurance until her fear has been heard.
items.fix: “That sounds terrifying — how are you doing?” Then the facts.

items.fail: Hedging: “It’s probably not epilepsy, but we can’t be completely sure.”
items.why: Vague answers to a specific fear leave the fear intact. For a simple febrile seizure the answer is clear.
items.fix: “This is not epilepsy and it has not damaged his brain.”

items.fail: Advising regular paracetamol to prevent another fit.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG143: antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions.
items.fix: “Calpol is for comfort — it doesn’t prevent these fits, and nothing you did caused this.”

items.fail: Not checking for complex features or meningitis because the child was seen this morning.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Things can change after an earlier assessment.
items.fix: Ask about focal features, duration, recovery, rash, neck stiffness and drowsiness, and observe him on video.

items.fail: No concrete plan for a recurrence — “bring him in if it happens again”.
items.why: The not-knowing is her biggest fear; non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Protect, don’t restrain, time it, recovery position, 999 at 5 minutes — and send it in writing.

items.fail: Ignoring “I don’t want to leave him alone again”.
items.why: Missed cue to parental trauma and hypervigilance that will persist without acknowledgement.
items.fix: Normalise it, give permission to let him sleep normally, and offer a review for her.

timeMap.d: She opens with “I thought he was dying”. Acknowledge that before any fact.
Look at Musa on camera. Generalised or focal, duration, recovery, any rash, neck stiffness, drowsiness or further fits.
Her fault for not lowering the fever; fear of leaving him; not knowing what to do. Name each.
Simple febrile convulsion: not epilepsy, no brain damage. Antipyretics don’t prevent fits. First aid with 999 at 5 minutes.
Written information, urgent features, support for her own shock. Teach-back: “What will you tell his dad?”

wordPics.fail: Launches into facts while she is still shaking; implies it may be epilepsy or says “we can’t be sure about the brain”; reinforces the idea that she should have controlled the fever; no first aid plan; no screen for meningitis.
wordPics.pass: Acknowledges her fear; confirms the simple pattern and full recovery; says clearly it is not epilepsy or brain damage; gives recurrence first aid and 999 criteria; safety-nets the fever.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explicitly lifts the guilt with the antipyretic fact; gently addresses hypervigilance and offers help if trauma persists; gives written information; checks understanding so she leaves feeling in control rather than frightened.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, febrile convulsions are very common.”
avoid.instead: “That sounds terrifying. I’m going to answer your questions clearly — first, how are you?”
avoid.why: Statistics before acknowledgement feel dismissive to a parent who thought her child was dying.

avoid.dont: “Try to keep his temperature down with Calpol so it doesn’t happen again.”
avoid.instead: “Calpol helps him feel comfortable, but it doesn’t prevent these fits. Nothing you did caused this.”
avoid.why: Reinforcing the myth deepens her guilt and is contrary to NICE NG143.

avoid.dont: “If it happens again, bring him in.”
avoid.instead: “Keep him safe, time it, on his side when it stops, and 999 if it lasts five minutes.”
avoid.why: Vague advice leaves her helpless; concrete first aid gives her control.

This is important. Calpol and ibuprofen make a child more comfortable, but they don’t prevent these fits. Nothing you did or didn’t do caused it. You didn’t fail him — you held him through it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Corrects the antipyretic myth and lifts the guilt (NICE NG143)

SCA_MODELS.text: I really thought I’d let it happen.

It can happen again with another fever, so let me give you a plan. If he fits: put him somewhere he can’t hurt himself, don’t hold him down and don’t put anything in his mouth. Look at the time. When the jerking stops, roll him onto his side. Call 999 if it lasts five minutes, if he has another one in the same illness, or if he doesn’t come round properly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Concrete first aid with explicit 999 criteria (NICE NG217)

SCA_MODELS.text: Five minutes. Time it. On his side.

Exactly. Carry on with his ear treatment. Give Calpol or ibuprofen only if he seems uncomfortable. He doesn’t need watching every second — he can sleep in his own cot tonight. Checking on him as you normally would is enough.
SCA_MODELS.why: Tailored plan that gently heads off hypervigilance

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t know if I’ll sleep, though.

A few bad nights after a shock like this is normal. If in a week or two you’re still getting flashbacks, can’t sleep or can’t leave him, please come back — that’s common after seeing something so frightening, and we can help with it.

I’ll send you written information on febrile convulsions and first aid, so you don’t have to remember it all. Please get help urgently if he becomes floppy or very drowsy, has a rash that doesn’t fade under a glass, a stiff neck, or is struggling to breathe.
SCA_MODELS.why: Written information plus named urgent features

SCA_MODELS.text: When you tell his dad tonight, what will you say happened and what you’d do next time?
That it was a fever fit, it’s not epilepsy, it didn’t hurt his brain, and it wasn’t my fault. If it happens: keep him safe, time it, on his side, 999 at five minutes.
That’s it exactly. You did everything right today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with reassurance that restores confidence

SCA_STEM.name: Musa
pmh: No previous seizures; no known family history
meds: Treatment for otitis media as recorded yesterday
SCA_STEM.recent: This morning: generalised convulsion lasting about 2 minutes during fever, stopped on its own, sleepy afterwards. Seen and assessed earlier today; now alert, playing and feeding. First child.
SCA_STEM.reason: Follow-up video call booked for the parents after his first febrile convulsion.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG143 (fever in under 5s) · NICE NG217 (epilepsies, 2022, updated January 2025) · NICE NG254 (sepsis, under 16s)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A brief, generalised, self-limiting seizure during a fever in a young child who recovers fully is a simple febrile seizure. It is frightening to watch but benign. The consultation is mostly about the parent’s shock, guilt and what to do next time.

points.t: Simple: generalised, brief, not repeated in the same illness, with full recovery. Complex features: focal, lasting longer than 15 minutes, repeated within the same illness or incomplete recovery. Complex febrile seizures carry a somewhat higher risk of later epilepsy and need paediatric assessment.

NICE NG217: febrile seizures tend not to predispose to later afebrile seizures, unlike a first afebrile seizure. A single simple febrile seizure does not mean epilepsy and does not harm the brain. Recurrence with later fevers is possible, and most children grow out of them.

NICE NG143: antipyretic agents do not prevent febrile convulsions and should not be used specifically for this purpose. Use them only for a distressed child. This directly answers the parent’s guilt that she “should have got the fever down faster”.

points.h: Look for the cause of the fever
points.t: Confirm the source (here, otitis media) and exclude serious infection. Features such as a non-blanching rash, neck stiffness, a bulging fontanelle, persistent drowsiness or incomplete recovery need urgent assessment. Use the NICE NG143 traffic-light approach and consider sepsis (NICE NG254).

Protect from injury, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, note the time, and place in the recovery position once the jerking stops. NICE NG217 defines convulsive status epilepticus as a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more: call 999 at 5 minutes, or for a second seizure in the same illness, breathing difficulty or failure to recover.

NICE NG217: give parents information about the risk of further seizures, how to seek help if one happens, and safety advice to reduce the risk of injury. Written information is essential after such a frightening event.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Asked how she was before the medical facts; heard the event and the questions in her own words.
First child, shock, sleeplessness, fear of leaving him, who is at home to support her.
Picked up “it’s me that isn’t” and “I should have got his temperature down”, and explored both.
Idea (epilepsy, brain damage, her fault), concern (recurrence and not knowing what to do), expectation (a clear answer).
Observed on video that he is alert and playing; checked the earlier assessment; no investigations needed for a simple febrile seizure with a clear source.
Simple vs complex febrile seizure; considered meningitis, sepsis and non-febrile causes.
Asked about rash, neck stiffness, drowsiness, vomiting and further seizures; confirmed generalised, brief, full recovery.
Simple febrile convulsion with otitis media, explained in plain words as benign and not epilepsy.
Corrected the antipyretic myth (NICE NG143), gave recurrence first aid with 999 at 5 minutes (NICE NG217), continued ear treatment.
Addressed parental trauma and hypervigilance; offered follow-up for her own wellbeing.
Written information, named urgent features (non-blanching rash, drowsiness, stiff neck, breathing), return if trauma persists.

social.t: Witnessing a seizure is often experienced as watching a child die. Sleeplessness, hypervigilance and intrusive memories are common in the days after and deserve acknowledgement.
Ask who is at home tonight. Sharing the first-aid plan with the other parent and any regular carers (nursery, grandparents) spreads the load and the knowledge.

legal.t: No legal restriction follows a single febrile seizure. Parents may wish to share the first-aid plan with nursery staff; this is their choice and needs their consent.

professional.t: Reassurance must be accurate: say clearly it is not epilepsy and has not harmed him, while being honest that it can recur (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: give information patients can understand).
A video follow-up is appropriate after an in-person assessment, but any new drowsiness, rash or further seizure needs face-to-face or emergency care. Document the advice given.

community.t: Written febrile convulsion and first-aid information; health visitor support for a first-time parent; paediatric first-aid courses (for example British Red Cross or St John Ambulance).

redFlags: Focal or prolonged seizure, a second seizure in the same illness, or incomplete recovery — complex features needing urgent assessment
Non-blanching rash, neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle, persistent drowsiness — meningitis or sepsis (NICE NG143, NICE NG254)
Seizure lasting 5 minutes or more — 999 (NICE NG217)
psychosocial: First child; parent in shock and not sleeping
Fear of leaving him alone, even to sleep
Who is at home tonight to support her
ice: Idea: “Is it epilepsy? Has it damaged his brain? I should have got the fever down.”
Concern: it will happen again and she won’t know what to do
Expectation: a clear answer about epilepsy and brain damage

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Simple febrile convulsion in an 18-month-old with acute otitis media: brief, generalised, self-terminating, single, with full recovery. No features of complex seizure or meningitis.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Musa had a fever fit — some young children’s brains react to a quickly rising temperature by having a short fit. It looks awful, but it doesn’t damage the brain, it isn’t epilepsy, and most children grow out of them.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been blaming yourself for not bringing his temperature down. Please hear this: medicines for fever don’t stop these fits. Nothing you did caused it.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the trauma, normalise a few bad nights, discourage constant watching, and offer a review for her if flashbacks or sleeplessness persist.
sharedPlan: Continue treatment for otitis media; antipyretics only for comfort (NICE NG143), doses per BNFC
First aid for recurrence: protect, don’t restrain, time it, recovery position, 999 at 5 minutes (NICE NG217)
Written information on febrile convulsions and first aid
safetyNet: 999 for a seizure lasting 5 minutes, a second seizure, not recovering, or breathing difficulty
Urgent help for non-blanching rash, stiff neck, floppiness or drowsiness; return if her distress persists

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The clinical content here is simple. The station is failed on sequence and tone: facts delivered to a parent still in shock, hedged answers to her two big questions, and a guilt that nobody lifts.

items.fail: Opening with “febrile convulsions are common and benign” before acknowledging what she saw.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” She cannot hear reassurance until her fear has been heard.
items.fix: “That sounds terrifying — how are you doing?” Then the facts.

items.fail: Hedging: “It’s probably not epilepsy, but we can’t be completely sure.”
items.why: Vague answers to a specific fear leave the fear intact. For a simple febrile seizure the answer is clear.
items.fix: “This is not epilepsy and it has not damaged his brain.”

items.fail: Advising regular paracetamol to prevent another fit.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG143: antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions.
items.fix: “Calpol is for comfort — it doesn’t prevent these fits, and nothing you did caused this.”

items.fail: Not checking for complex features or meningitis because the child was seen this morning.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Things can change after an earlier assessment.
items.fix: Ask about focal features, duration, recovery, rash, neck stiffness and drowsiness, and observe him on video.

items.fail: No concrete plan for a recurrence — “bring him in if it happens again”.
items.why: The not-knowing is her biggest fear; non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Protect, don’t restrain, time it, recovery position, 999 at 5 minutes — and send it in writing.

items.fail: Ignoring “I don’t want to leave him alone again”.
items.why: Missed cue to parental trauma and hypervigilance that will persist without acknowledgement.
items.fix: Normalise it, give permission to let him sleep normally, and offer a review for her.
